newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia farm industry calls for export credits.
newsitem.headline: Serbia farm industry calls for export credits.

text.p: Serbia's agriculture industry called on the republican government and its Development Fund to speed up allocation of credits to save the ailing sector and finance export-oriented production.

"They should at least tell us whether or not credits will be available and not keep leading us on," Jovan Pekic of Poljoprivreda Sombor farm complex told a meeting in the Serbian Chamber of Commerce on Thursday.
The Fund is the recipient of nearly $1 billion from the sale of a 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija telecommunications company to Italian and Greek partners earlier this month.
The Serbian government aims to double exports this year by financing related industry through the Fund.

Although agriculture is seen as a potentially high hard currency earner, with the sector's exports for 1997 forecast at around $700 million, industry sources complained they had not seen any money yet.

The agriculture sector joined other industry branches in clamouring for much-needed credits to boost production, but independent analysts feared the funds would be channelled to companies with close ties to the government.
The sector is on the brink of collapse. Machinery is old and exhausted, farmers have not been paid for last year's crops and high interest rates on credits have multiplied their debts several-fold.

Of the 800 million dinars owed to farmers by the state and processing industry for last year's crops, 685 million, or 86 percent, have been repaid so far, the Chamber's Agriculture Committee said in its report.
Serbia's Commodity Reserve Agency still owed farmers some 50 million and sugar and oil refineries and tobacco and wine producers 64 million dinars, the report said.

The acute problem of financing spring sowing was eased partially under Serbian government and National Bank of Yugoslavia decisions to allow the sector to postpone payments of taxes and contributions until the end of November.

The central bank and government also decided to extend farmers' obligations stemming from primary issue until the end of the year and to redirect part of banks' reserves into primary agricultural production.
But stable and certain sources of finance for primary agriculture have not been found yet.

According to the report, raw materials needed for farm works include 1.086 million tonnes of artificial fertilizer, 100,000 tonnes of diesel fuel, 21,000 tonnes of seed maize and 10,000 tonnes of pesticides and herbicides worth some 3.043 billion dinars, 1.217 billion of which for processing industry.

Some 400,000 tractors and auxiliary equipment had to be overhauled, but the problem of worn machinery and spare parts remains acute. The average age of Serbia's estimated 19,500 combines and 4,000 harvesters is 11-1/2 years.
The Serbian goverment's decision on exchange of farm produce for raw materials, fuel and agricultural machinery through the Commodity Reserve Agency is behind plan.

"Despite all the losses and difficulties, the country had enough produce last year for its own needs, for the processing industry and for exports, and we have managed to complete this spring sowing in very complex circumstances," Bogdan Obradovic of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce Agriculture Committee said.
But other industry sources were not so optimistic.

"Agriculture is in collapse and so is part of the food processing industry. Unless we take measures to consolidate it, we will have serious problems this year," said Dragan Milivojevic of Serbia's biggest farm complex Poljoprivredni Kombinat Beograd (PKB).
Wheat harvesting on some 800,000 hectares in Yugoslavia is expected to begin next week.
-- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
